titulo.texto: Jew Mask / Dance of the Cora of Holy Week

frase_gancho.texto: A fierce mask for a theater where the Sun descends to the land of the dead.

puente_narrativo.texto: We leave the dry sierra behind and head to the lakes of Michoacán. Look for a house of pine planks, with a four-sided roof and a loft, built without a single nail.

guion_corto.texto: This mask is worn during the Holy Week of the Cora, or náayeri, a people of the sierra of Nayarit, who call it the Judea. The men who wear it represent the “Jews,” characters who persecute Christ; among the Cora they are also understood as forces of the night and the stars. The mask has fierce features, and it is painted to frighten. Whoever puts it on stops being himself and becomes another being. In the Judea, the persecution and death of Christ blend with a very ancient idea: that the Sun must be reborn for the rain to come and the maize to grow.

guion_largo.texto:
To put on a mask is to change your being. The Teotihuacán, the Mexica, and the Maya knew this, and the Cora, or náayeri, neighbors of the Wixárika in the Gran Nayar sierra, still know it today. This mask belongs to their Holy Week, which they call the Judea, a ceremony that lasts several days and brings together entire towns.

To understand it, you have to look at two worlds. On one side, the religious drama of Holy Week brought by the European friars, in which the “Jews” were the enemies of Jesus. On the other, the worldview of the Cora, whose language, náayeri, is related to that of the Wixárika and, more distantly, to Nahuatl: all three belong to the Uto-Aztecan family, in which the Sun and the rain depend on ceremonies. The Cora took on the role of the “Jew” and filled it with their own meaning. Today the word refers to a character in this festival, not to any real person.

The men who play the “Jews,” who are also called “the painted ones,” cover their bodies with paint and put on these masks. They run, they mock, they chase. They represent forces of the night and of the stars, which in this story pursue the Sun. The fierce mask serves that purpose: so that no one sees the young man from the community, but a being who comes from somewhere else.

And what happens to the Sun? It dies and is born again. It is an idea you already know. In the Popol Vuh, the twins descend to the underworld and return transformed into the Sun and the Moon. Here we do not know whether there is a direct connection, but the pattern is similar: the light has to descend into darkness in order to return. Some scholars think that the Cora Judea speaks of that cycle, and of the arrival of the rains in the sierra.

There is something else to learn. The Cora resisted the Spaniards for a very long time. Their sierra was among the last areas of the west to be subdued, in the eighteenth century, nearly two hundred years after the fall of Tenochtitlan. Perhaps that is why their ceremony has kept so much strength of its own: it is the result of a people who chose what to accept and what to preserve.

Notice how the look of a mask changes depending on who is looking at it. For a visitor, it is a work of art; for the dancer, a tool of transformation; for the community, a part of a cycle that guarantees the world keeps turning. The museum shows it behind glass, but its natural place is movement. Imagine the noise that goes with it: running, shouting, the nervous laughter of those watching, and the drum in the background. A still mask is only half of the story.

In the next hall you will see another mask, very different: smiling, pink, and mocking. Among the Cora and the Purépecha, the same object, the mask, serves both to fear and to laugh.

texto: Look for the fierce features of the face: how do they make you feel?
Observe the colors and the painted designs

texto.Region: Mesa del Nayar / Jesús María, Sierra de Nayarit
texto.Technique/Material: Papier-mâché, natural deer/goat horns, horsehair, pigments, and cloth
texto.Function: Ritual masking paraphernalia for the processional dance of the Judea

texto.pregunta: Myth: The masks of Indigenous dances are just festival costumes.
texto.respuesta: Reality: For those who wear them, they are a way of transforming into another being. In the Cora Judea they are part of a ceremony about the death and rebirth of the Sun.
